Learning Objectives
Define the term functionally irreparable rotator cuff tear.
Understand the pathoanatomy, etiology, and risk factors of a functionally irreparable rotator
cuff tear.
Discuss several joint-preserving surgical treatment options for young patients with a
functionally irreparable rotator cuff tear.
Review the indications, techniques, and outcomes of several tendon transfer procedures.

Rotator cuff tears commonly are associated with pain and dysfunction. Typically, nonsurgical
management, such as physical therapy, or primary surgical repair are viable treatment
options.1-4
A massive and irreparable rotator cuff tear is a completely different entity and is a challenge to
manage.
In such a scenario, reverse total shoulder arthroplasty is associated with favorable outcomes
in the elderly population.5,6
Arthroplasty is not indicated for active, young patients with intact articular cartilage.
Joint-preserving treatment options include débridement, partial repair, balloon implantation,
graft interposition, and superior capsule reconstruction. Some controversy exists regarding
these procedures.7,8
Tendon transfer is another option used to improve shoulder mechanics and quality of life;
however, it is technically challenging (Video 1).

The terms massive and irreparable are not comprehensive terms to describe this challenging
pathology or its joint-preserving procedures, such as tendon transfer.5
The term functionally irreparable rotator cuff tear (FIRCT) is a more applicable term.

Definitions
Typically, surgeons used the terms massive or irreparable in characterizing a rotator cuff
tear that cannot be repaired primarily; however, these terms may not capture the full
extent of the structural pathoanatomy and nature of the disease.5 For example, because
the term massive solely refers to size, an acute tear that encompasses the entire rotator
cuff can be characterized as massive but often is repairable. In addition, a chronic
tendon tear with extensive fatty infiltration and muscle atrophy may be repairable in the
sense that the tendon can be fixed onto its insertion site; however, a repair of this
nature would lead to unfavorable clinical outcomes with poor tendon healing.9-12
Therefore, the terms, massive and irreparable, are inadequate for defining the full
extent of the disease; neither terms should be used interchangeably. The term FIRCT is
used to more aptly describe a tear in an active patient in whom primary rotator cuff
repair failed because of pathoanatomy, such as muscle and tendon quality, or other
patient-related factors. In addition, the term FIRCT is more applicable in evaluating and
analyzing joint-preserving procedures.
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Surgeons must be able to evaluate and diagnose patients with FIRCT.
Patient history, physical examination, imaging studies, and recognition of concurrent
diagnoses are key components.13-19

Evaluation and Diagnosis
A thorough patient history and physical examination are the initial steps in diagnosing a
FIRCT. Common symptoms include pain at night, constant pain, limited range of motion,

poor overhead function, decreased strength, and low satisfaction.13,20 During the
patient history, a detailed account of previous shoulder surgeries and the status of
preoperative function, including work status and limitation of daily activities, are
imperative. The physical examination involves evaluation of muscle atrophy, abnormal
scapulothoracic motion, active and passive range of motion, strength, the cervical spine,
and neurovascular status.
If the patient history and physical examination findings are concerning for a FIRCT, then
imaging, including radiography, MRI, CT arthrography, magnetic resonance
arthrography, and ultrasonography, are the next diagnostic step. The ability of MRI to
reveal a FIRCT or failed rotator cuff repair ranges from 70% to 90%, and the accuracy can
be improved with intra-articular contrast.14-17 Ultrasonography also may be used to
evaluate the integrity of a previous repair; however, its accuracy largely operator
dependent.21 These imaging modalities can help surgeons evaluate the articular
cartilage using the Hamada Classification of Massive Rotator Cuff Tears, tendon length,
and the quality of the rotator cuff musculature.
Potential concurrent diagnoses, which must be recognized and considered, include
adhesive capsulitis, glenohumeral and acromioclavicular joint arthritis, biceps disease,
suprascapular nerve compression, scapulothoracic dyskinesia, deltoid injuries, infection,
fracture, and cervical spine pathology.13,18,19,22 The diagnostic workup for these
concurrent pathologies ranges from electromyography and diagnostic injections to
inflammatory markers, such as C-reactive protein level, white blood cell count, and
erythrocyte sedimentation rate.19,23-25 Treatment options include arthroscopic or open
procedures, such as capsular release and biceps tenodesis/tenotomy, decompression of
the suprascapular nerve, deltoidplasty, and extensive débridement for
infection.19,23,24,26,27
After a diagnosis of a FIRCT is made, the treating surgeon must understand that several
risk factors exist for failed primary rotator cuff repair. Inability to recognize these
contributing factors may lead to poor results with joint-preserving procedures for this
challenging problem. Therefore, a discussion of these risk factors is warranted.

Risk Factors for Failed Primary Rotator Cuff Repair
Primary rotator cuff repair failure may occur because of structural failure or patient-related
factors.28
Various risk factors, including rotator cuff damage and patient-related factors, may contribute
to an increased likelihood of failed primary rotator cuff repair.

Risk Factors for Failed Primary Rotator Cuff Repair
All failed primary rotator cuff repair procedures are associated with contributing
structural and patient-related risk factors. Structural damage to the rotator cuff
musculature has been implicated as an important risk factor. Another risk factor, the size
of the tear, directly correlates with clinical outcomes.10,28,29 Massive rotator cuff tears
are defined by Cofield1 as those larger than 5 cm in size. Gerber et al2 defined massive
rotator cuff tears as those involving two or more tendons. Nobuhara et al3 further
defined the size of tears by the amount of humeral head exposed. Other structural risk
factors include tendon retraction, decreased tendon length, locations correlated with a
poorer prognosis (muscle-tendon junction, involvement of the lower subscapularis and
teres minor), articular involvement, muscle atrophy, and fatty infiltration.11,30-32
Depending on the extent of rotator cuff damage, imaging studies may reveal decreased
acromial-tuberosity distance for posterosuperior rotator cuff tears (superior humeral
head migration) or anterior subluxation of the humeral head relative to the glenoid for
subscapularis tears.31,32
Patient-related factors play an important role in the failure of primary rotator cuff repair.
Advanced age is associated with osteoporotic bone, decreased tendon-bone healing, and
poor vascularity.19,33-35 Other risk factors include mental health issues, such as
depression, reduced preoperative range of motion, smoking; diabetes mellitus,
hyperlipidemia, patient compliance, workers’ compensation claims, revision surgery, and
pseudoparalysis.36-44 Tokish et al39 and Tokish and Brinkman45 refined the definition of
pseudoparalysis to include 0° of active elevation with free passive elevation and
anterosuperior escape of the humerus, dissimilar from pseudoparesis, which is defined
as less than 90° of active elevation with full passive elevation sustained from an

irreparable rotator cuff tear.39 In addition, steroid injections may lead to an increased
risk for infection or failed repair.46 Overall, understanding the factors contributing to
primary rotator cuff repair failure promotes the recognition of a FIRCT.
In the elderly patient population, reverse total shoulder arthroplasty is associated with
favorable outcomes;5,6 however, arthroplasty is not indicated in active, young patients
with intact articular cartilage. Therefore, the decision to pursue joint-preserving
procedures must be made.
Implications for Joint-Preserving Procedures
The decision to pursue joint-preserving procedures depends on the structural integrity of the
rotator cuff and several patient-related factors.

Implications for Joint-Preserving Procedures
After the clinical evaluation and imaging studies have been completed and the clinician
has recognized the structural and patient-related risk factors for failure, several
implications for joint-preserving procedures must be considered. Shimokobe et al47
reported that lack of active preoperative motion—specifically preoperative active
external rotation less than 25°—was an important risk factor for failed primary repair of
posterosuperior large or massive tears. Burnier et al48 reviewed a treatment algorithm
and reported favoring joint-preserving procedures in patients with a rotator cuff tear
encompassing two or more tendons with any of the following characteristics: substantial
fatty infiltration, tendon retraction beyond the rim of the glenoid, length less than 15
mm as observed on MRI, a muscle-tendon junction of the infraspinatus, or failed well-
fixed repair. Reverse total shoulder arthroplasty is associated with favorable clinical
outcomes in elderly patients; however, joint-preserving options should be considered
initially in younger patients with a FIRCT and an intact articular surface.5,6
Joint-Preserving Procedures Other Than Tendon Transfers

Nonsurgical management and joint-preserving procedures other than tendon transfers
include débridement/acromioplasty/biceps tenotomy or tenodesis, balloon implantation, graft
interposition, superior capsule reconstruction, and partial rotator cuff repair.
The literature has shown mixed results and outcomes with these treatment options; therefore,
patient selection is key.

Joint-Preserving Procedures Other Than Tendon Transfers
For FIRCTs, nonsurgical management centers on physical therapy, specifically deltoid
conditioning and periscapular muscles, such as the latissimus dorsi and the pectoralis
major; strengthening; anti-inflammatory medications; and possibly corticosteroid
injections.8,22 If nonsurgical management fails, then several joint-preserving surgical
treatment options other than tendon transfers are available for young and active
patients with a FIRCT. Arthroscopic and open débridement, acromioplasty, and/or biceps
tenodesis/tenotomy are associated with improved pain scores.49-51 However, some
studies have reported concerns, such as biceps cramping, the risk for anterosuperior
escape after coracoacromial release and acromioplasty, and progression of rotator cuff
tears and weakness.52,53
Another treatment option is balloon implantation in the subacromial space, which
involves the use of an inflatable device composed of copolymer poly-DL-lactide and poly-
L-lactide-co-ε-caprolactone material. The device degrades over 12 months, but the
rationale focuses on centering/depressing the humeral head to allow for functional use
of the rotator cuff force couples and prevention of superior humeral head migration.
Several studies have reported favorable clinical outcomes.54,55 Prat et al56 reported a
46% satisfaction rate, with a complication rate of 16.7% in a series of 24 patients treated
via balloon implantation. Insufficiency of the subscapularis appears to be a
contraindication because of concerns for anterior migration of the balloon.57
Augmentation and interposition with grafts, such as biceps, fascia lata autograft, human
dermal collagen matrix allograft, and synthetic material, can reduce the gap between the
tendon edge and its footprint during rotator cuff repair.56,58 Theorized advantages
include improved structural strength and healing potential.59 Lewington et al60 reported

favorable functional outcomes, improved pain scores, and better graft survival in a
review of the literature on allografts and xenografts. Sunwoo and Murrell61 reported
promising outcomes 2 years after graft interposition regardless of graft type.
Mihata et al62 introduced the concept of superior capsular reconstruction, which
involves using fascia lata autograft for interposed tissue stabilization between the
humeral head and the acromion in massive rotator cuff tears. Other tissue choices
include acellular dermal allograft and biceps tendon. Varying outcomes have been
observed for the type of graft chosen for fixation.63,64 Although Mihata et al65 reported
improved flexion, external rotation, and internal rotation in 23 patients in whom a fascia
lata autograft was used, Lee and Min40 reported a 36.1% re-tear rate in a series of 36
shoulders managed with the use of fascia lata autograft or dermal allograft. In addition,
Denard et al63 reported a 18.6% revision rate in a cohort of 59 patients treated with the
use of a dermal allograft. Improved outcomes suggest the importance of an adequate
posterior rotator cuff and fixation of the graft to any remnant of the posterosuperior
rotator cuff.
Tendon Transfers
Tendon transfers are technically challenging but are a viable treatment option for restoring
shoulder mechanics and improving quality of life in patients with a FIRCT.22
For posterosuperior rotator cuff tears, latissimus dorsi, teres major, or lower trapezius tendon
transfers are surgical treatment options.66-71
Pectoralis major, pectoralis minor, or anterior latissimus dorsi tendon transfers can be used to
manage irreparable anterosuperior rotator cuff tears.71-73
Combined latissimus dorsi and teres major tendon transfers can address external rotation.
A contraindication for tendon transfer in patients with posterior cuff deficiency is Hamada
stage 3 or greater.
A relative contraindication for tendon transfer in patients with subscapularis deficiency is fixed
anterior subluxation of the humeral head.
Arthroscopic-assisted techniques exist for most of these tendon transfers 49,54,67,68,70,71,72,73-
82 (Table 1).

The irreparable posterosuperior rotator cuff tear initially described by Gerber 83 is
defined as the inability to achieve adequate primary fixation of the tear with the
shoulder in less than 60° of abduction. The definition also involves extensive fatty
infiltration of the supraspinatus/infraspinatus, an acromiohumeral distance of less than
7 mm, and a fixed superiorly migrated humeral head.73,84 Conversely, anterosuperior
rotator cuff tears mostly consist of the subscapularis and are less common than
previously mentioned posterosuperior rotator cuff tears.85,86 A radiographic study of
2,000 patients with a rotator cuff tear found that subscapularis tears only represented
2%.87 The subscapularis provides anterior stabilization of the glenohumeral joint and
acts as an important internal rotator. Ultimately, these pathologies lead to loss of
shoulder mechanics and decreased quality of life.
Massive and irreparable rotator cuff tears lead to the loss of dynamic centering forces
onto the glenoid, which may accelerate glenohumeral joint wear. In younger patients
with a FIRCT, various tendon transfers can be performed, depending on the type of
irreparable tear; however, the core principles are the same. The donor tendon must be
expendable, with appropriate strength (at best, one level less than original strength), and
have adequate excursion, along with synergism. In addition, the glenohumeral joint
should be supple enough to allow for the transfer. Overall, the tendon transfer becomes
a source of vascularity, compression, and power. Arthroscopic-assisted techniques also
exist for most of these transfers.22,48
Latissimus Dorsi Tendon Transfer
Latissimus dorsi tendon transfer is a surgical treatment option associated with favorable
clinical and functional outcomes for irreparable posterosuperior rotator cuff
tears.48,67,69,74,75,84
Young patients with an intact subscapularis/teres minor and active elevation greater than 80°
are ideal surgical candidates48 (Videos 2 and 3).

Latissimus dorsi tendon transfer can reduce humeral head migration and restore
external rotation in patients with an irreparable posterosuperior rotator cuff tear. The
tendon has a potential excursion of 33 mm.76 The transfer itself is associated with
excellent strength and posterior force couple but exhibits poor synergism. Gerber et al84
initially described a two-incision technique. Via a superior incision over the acromion, the
deltoid is partially detached with a piece of bone to allow for exposure of the insertions
of the posterosuperior rotator cuffs. Any remnant rotator cuff musculature is repaired or
incorporated into the transfer. Then, via a second incision over the axilla, the latissimus
dorsi tendon is carefully harvested off the humerus, and Krackow stitches with
nonabsorbable sutures are incorporated into the tendon. The tendon is mobilized under
the deltoid and fixed onto the greater tuberosity. Modifications to the original technique
have been made. Habermeyer et al88 reported on a single-incision approach that
involves more posterior exposure of the humeral head, whereas Herzberg et al76
described fixing the transfer onto the infraspinatus insertion via a single V-shaped
incision over the axillary and posterior humerus. The ideal insertion site of the transfer
remains controversial.78 Fixation to the anterior aspect of the greater tuberosity or the
subscapularis improves humeral head coverage and compression effect, whereas
attachment to the infraspinatus insertion contributes to improved external rotation and
elevation.76,89-93 Grimberg et al67 reported comparable outcomes between
arthroscopic-assisted and open techniques.
Gerber83 reported 74% good or excellent outcomes via a two-incision technique in a
study population with a mean follow-up of 10 years. El-Azab et al94 reported improved
pain scores and increased strength and function in a cohort of 93 patients with a mean
follow-up of 9 years. Castricini et al74 reported favorable clinical outcomes in patients
treated via arthroscopic-assisted techniques. Conversely, progression of arthritis has
been reported, and poorer outcomes have been associated with prior rotator cuff repair,
pseudoparalysis, subscapularis/teres minor tears, and active elevation less than
80°.67,69,75,83,95 Complications include adhesive capsulitis, structural failure of the
transfer, nerve injuries, and deltoid reattachment failure.96,97

Combined Latissimus Dorsi and Teres Major Tendon Transfer
Latissimus dorsi tendon and teres major tendon transfer is associated with satisfactory
outcomes, with functional gains in external rotation in patients with a posterosuperior FIRCT
and brachial plexus palsy.53,88,97
Poorer outcomes are associated with a nonfunctional subscapularis.

Combined Latissimus Dorsi and Teres Major Tendon Transfer
Combined latissimus dorsi and teres major tendon transfer to the humerus was
described originally by L’Episcopo97 to help restore external rotation in patients with
brachial plexus palsy. For the management of a FIRCT, Habermeyer et al88 added an
incision on the posterior aspect of the deltoid to avoid detachment and reported
improved external rotation and flexion in a cohort of 20 patients. Performing the
transfer via a deltopectoral approach to the posterolateral humerus, Boileau et al53
reported an 84% satisfaction rate and a mean increase of 26° of external rotation.
Poorer outcomes are associated with a nonfunctional subscapularis. Boughebri et al79
also reported few complications and considerably increased external rotation. This
transfer combination also may be performed in the setting of reverse total shoulder
arthroplasty with an external rotation lag sign.
Lower Trapezius Tendon Transfer
Early results of lower trapezius tendon transfer are promising for patients with an irreparable
posterosuperior tear, and this technique has become a successful alternative to latissimus
dorsi tendon transfer.48
Poorer outcomes are associated with subscapularis insufficiency; however, fatty infiltration of
the teres minor does not affect outcomes70 (Videos 4 and 5).

Lower Trapezius Tendon Transfer
The lower trapezius has good strength and synergism, with a moment arm in a similar
orientation to the infraspinatus; however, an allograft, usually an Achilles tendon, must
be used for transfer to the greater tuberosity because of the inadequate length and
amplitude of the lower trapezius tendon. In addition, the moment arm for external
rotation has been shown to be biomechanically stronger for the lower trapezius in
adduction than the superior strength of the latissimus dorsi in abduction.98
The original technique involves a two-incision approach, in which the first incision
involves exposure of the posterosuperior humeral head with deltoid take down. The
second incision is started 1 cm medial to the scapula to harvest and detach the lower
trapezius tendon from the scapular spine. After the tendon is fully mobilized, it is
augmented with an Achilles tendon allograft and passed from the medial incision to the
lateral incision under the deltoid. Then, the transfer is fixed onto the insertion sites of
the supraspinatus and the upper aspect of the infraspinatus.22,48 Recently, arthroscopic-
assisted techniques have been used with this technique.
Regarding outcomes, Elhassan et al70 reported a considerable increase in range of
motion, especially in forward flexion, abduction, and external rotation, in 33 patients
with a FIRCT managed via arthroscopic-assisted lower trapezius transfer. The authors
also concluded that poorer outcomes were associated with subscapularis insufficiency;
however, fatty infiltration of the teres minor did not affect outcomes. The most common
complication in the study was seroma from the subcutaneous tunneling for the transfer.
Donegan et al99 also reported substantial improvement in outcome measures, pain,
external rotation, and flexion in a series of 12 patients.

Pectoralis major tendon transfer provides an internal rotation centering force for irreparable
subscapularis tears; however, reported outcomes reveal mixed results.72,80,81,82

Pectoralis Major Tendon Transfer
Transfer of the clavicular head, the sternal head, or the superior aspect of the pectoralis
major is indicated for a FIRCT of the subscapularis. The original technique described by
Gerber et al82 involves transfer of the pectoralis major to the lesser tuberosity anterior
to the conjoint tendon. Resch et al100 later modified the technique by using the
clavicular head of the pectoralis major under the conjoint tendon, reporting
considerable improvement in functional status and pain scores in 12 patients with a
follow-up of 28 months. Warner101 described transferring the inferior aspect of the
sternal head of the pectoralis major under the clavicular head anterior to the conjoint
tendon, avoiding injury to musculocutaneous nerve.
Moroder et al80 reported a 77% satisfaction rate in a series of 27 patients followed for 10
years. Klepps et al102 reported a 75% satisfaction rate with improved functional scores.
Despite these favorable results, Gavriilidis et al81 reported no improvement in shoulder
motion in 15 patients followed for 37 months. In addition, Elhassan et al72 reported
seven structural failures in 22 patients treated via transfer of the sternal head of the
pectoralis major. The authors suggested that the transfer is ideal in patients younger
than 65 years who have an intact or reparable posterosuperior rotator cuff tears and
minimal arthritis. A loss of external rotation may be expected because of the tenodesis
effect of the transfer.100
Pectoralis Minor Tendon Transfer
Pectoralis minor tendon transfer is indicated for irreparable anterosuperior rotator cuff tears.

Pectoralis minor tendon transfer is an option for irreparable anterosuperior rotator cuff
tears and was originally described by Wirth and Rockwood in 1997.103 Paladini et al71
later described a subcoracoid pectoralis minor transfer with a small piece of the coracoid
inserted onto the insertion of the subscapularis, reporting substantial improvement in
forward flexion and outcomes scores and an increased return to daily activities in 27
patients.
Anterior Latissimus Dorsi Tendon Transfer
The latissimus dorsi tendon is transferred anteriorly to the lesser tuberosity for the
management of irreparable anterosuperior tears.
Studies on this technique are limited66 (Video 6).

The latissimus dorsi tendon may offer a comparable line of pull with adequate strength
and excursion for the management of anterosuperior tears. Studies have shown that
transfer of the pectoralis major or minor may not fully replicate the line of pull of the
subscapularis because both of their origins are in the anterior chest. Elhassan et al66
reported that the transfer can be performed via open or arthroscopic techniques
without extensive compression of the axillary, radial, and musculocutaneous nerves. The
only outcome study that has evaluated this technique was conducted by Kany et al.77
Pearls/Pitfalls
Management of FIRCTs is a challenge, especially in young patients.
Performing a thorough diagnostic workup, including imaging studies and a clinical
examination, and recognizing structural and patient-related risk factors for failed primary
rotator cuff repair are critical to maximize patient outcomes.
Joint-preserving procedures include débridement, balloon implantation, graft interposition,
and superior capsule reconstruction.
Tendon transfers are technically demanding but have been shown to improve quality of life
and shoulder biomechanics.
Latissimus dorsi, teres major, and lower trapezius tendon transfers can be performed to
manage irreparable posterosuperior rotator cuff tears.
Pectoralis major, pectoralis minor, and anterior latissimus dorsi tendon transfers can be
performed to manage irreparable anterosuperior rotator cuff tears.
